metadata.title: Peer Effects in Education: Theoretical Synthesis of Frame Factor Theory and Opportunity to Learn using TIMSS 2011

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses Swedish TIMSS 2011 data for 8th-grade mathematics, with a gross sample of 5,816 students and a net analytic sample of 3,928 students after excluding outlier class sizes and classes with more than one mathematics teacher. The authors report that data were weighted using “house weights” on the between-class level (Rutkowski et al., 2010), which is intended to support correct estimation under the nested school/class sampling structure. The analysis is conducted with multilevel structural equation modelling (M-SEM) in Mplus, which relies on the specified weighting approach rather than replicate-weight variance estimation. No replicate-weight method (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is reported, so uncertainty quantification is described through the SEM framework and robust estimation rather than explicit replicate procedures.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper uses TIMSS plausible values for mathematics achievement (BSMMATH01–05) and describes how Mplus runs the model across plausible values and reports mean effects, but it does not explicitly document a separate missing-data strategy for questionnaire/indicator variables beyond the reported sample exclusions (e.g., class size and multiple-teacher exclusions) and the use of latent variables. Because the missing-data handling for the remaining indicators is not clearly specified (e.g., listwise vs. FIML/MI for non-PV missingness), this is a reporting gap. The results should therefore be interpreted with caution regarding how missing responses in the teacher/student questionnaires were treated within the SEM estimation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used Swedish TIMSS 2011 (8th grade, mathematics) student test results and teacher survey data. The gross sample included 153 schools, 266 classes, and 5,816 students; classes with fewer than 10 or more than 40 students were excluded as outliers. Classes with more than one mathematics teacher were excluded to avoid ambiguity in selecting which teacher’s OTL/peer-related instruction measures to use. The resulting net sample contained 134 schools, 207 classes, and 3,928 students. For teacher limitation indicators, two limitation variables (lack of nutrition; lack of sleep) were not used due to extensive missingness; the remaining four were used to form the latent “Limitations on Instruction” construct.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2011 Sweden Grade 8 Mathematics (BSMMATH01–05 plausible values)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel SEM (M-SEM) coefficients and fit indices: LIMIT → achievement standardized effect about -0.54 to -0.65 across M1–M3 (p < .05); ADV_CONTENT → achievement standardized effect about 0.15 to 0.19 across M1–M3 (p < .05). Model fit reported for measurement model: RMSEA ≈ 0.031, CFI ≈ 0.977, SRMR within ≈ 0.026 and between ≈ 0.056. Explained variance (R2 for achievement) in M1–M3: 0.115, 0.120, 0.113; ICC for achievement in empty model ≈ 17.1%.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2011 Sweden Grade 8 Mathematics data (BSMMATH01–05 plausible values), the study leveraged Limitations on instruction (LIMIT), Advanced content coverage (ADV_CONTENT), Class mean SES (CLASS_SES), Age of coming to Sweden (AGE_OF_COMING), and Instruction according to students (S_INSTR) to model mathematics achievement, finding that Limitations on instruction had a substantial negative relation with achievement (standardized about -0.54 to -0.65, p < .05) while Advanced content coverage had a small positive relation (standardized about 0.15 to 0.19, p < .05). This indicates that peer-composition-related constraints on instruction may be a key mechanism for between-class achievement differences, suggesting that equity policies should target instructional time/coverage and classroom-level instructional constraints rather than only improving teacher quality in isolation.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes Swedish TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 mathematics using student plausible values (BSMMATH01–05) and teacher/student survey items to test a synthesized Frame Factor Theory (FFT) and Opportunity to Learn (OTL) model of peer effects. The analytic sample is 3,928 students in 207 classes after excluding outlier class sizes (<10 or >40 students) and classes with more than one mathematics teacher; teacher limitation indicators with extensive missingness (lack of nutrition; lack of sleep) are omitted from the latent construct. The authors estimate a multilevel structural equation model (M-SEM) in Mplus with MLR and handle plausible values by running the model across each PV and reporting mean effects. Results show that the latent “Limitations on instruction” is strongly negatively related to mathematics achievement (standardized about -0.54 to -0.65, p < .05), while “Advanced content coverage” has a small positive relation (about 0.15–0.19, p < .05). Because the design is cross-sectional and the paper does not fully specify non-PV missing-data handling, causal claims are limited and should be interpreted as theory-consistent evidence rather than causal proof.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This paper is an empirical theory-testing study using multilevel structural equation modelling (SEM/M-SEM) rather than machine-learning predictive modelling. As a result, no ML algorithms (e.g., Random Forest, XGBoost) are evaluated, and the ML technique fields are intentionally left empty. The extraction therefore focuses on the SEM-based relationships among latent constructs and achievement, which are reported via standardized path coefficients and SEM fit statistics rather than ML performance metrics.
